claim: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior (RRBs).
source: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by two major diagnostic criteria – persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and the presence of restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior (RRBs).
evidence: This is a standard clinical definition of ASD based on established diagnostic criteria.

claim: Alteration of striatal circuits may contribute to the manifestation of RRBs in ASD.
source: Evidence from both human and animal model studies of ASD suggests that alteration of striatal circuits, which mediate motor learning, action selection, and habit formation, may contribute to the manifestation of RRBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior human and animal studies.

claim: CNTNAP2 is a syndromic ASD risk gene.
source: CNTNAP2 is a syndromic ASD risk gene, and loss of function of Cntnap2 in mice is associated with RRBs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CNTNAP2's role in ASD.

claim: Loss of function of Cntnap2 in mice is associated with RRBs.
source: CNTNAP2 is a syndromic ASD risk gene, and loss of function of Cntnap2 in mice is associated with RRBs.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on Cntnap2 mouse models.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortical drive of direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs).
source: We find that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortical drive of direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Enhanced cortical drive in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is due to increased intrinsic excitability of dSPNs.
source: This enhanced drive is due to increased intrinsic excitability of dSPNs, which make them more responsive to cortical inputs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased excitability measurements.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit spontaneous repetitive behaviors.
source: We find that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit spontaneous repetitive behaviors, increased motor routine learning, perseveration, and cognitive inflexibility.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit increased motor routine learning.
source: We find that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit spontaneous repetitive behaviors, increased motor routine learning, perseveration, and cognitive inflexibility.
evidence: This is supported by rotarod task data.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit perseveration.
source: We find that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit spontaneous repetitive behaviors, increased motor routine learning, perseveration, and cognitive inflexibility.
evidence: This is supported by reversal learning task data.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit cognitive inflexibility.
source: We find that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit spontaneous repetitive behaviors, increased motor routine learning, perseveration, and cognitive inflexibility.
evidence: This is supported by reversal learning task data.

claim: Increased corticostriatal drive may contribute to the acquisition of repetitive, inflexible behaviors in Cntnap2 mice.
source: Increased corticostriatal drive may therefore contribute to the acquisition of repetitive, inflexible behaviors in Cntnap2 mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the physiological and behavioral findings.

claim: ASD has high heritability.
source: Given that ASD has high heritability (Sandin et al., 2017), much work has been done in the last 30 years to identify genes that confer risk of developing ASD (De Rubeis et al., 2014; Iossifov et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sandin et al., 2017.

claim: Hundreds of high-confidence ASD risk genes have been identified.
source: Through this, hundreds of high-confidence risk genes have been identified, varying greatly in the proteins for which they code (Satterstrom et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Satterstrom et al., 2020.

claim: ASD risk genes include transcriptional and translational regulators, ion channels, receptors, cell adhesion molecules, and others.
source: These include transcriptional and translational regulators, ion channels, receptors, cell adhesion molecules, and others (De Rubeis et al., 2014; Delorme et al., 2013; Ebert and Greenberg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The striatum represents a commonly altered brain region in ASD.
source: The basal ganglia, in particular the striatum, represents one such commonly altered brain region, and prior studies have demonstrated changes in striatal function and striatum-associated behaviors in mice with mutations in ASD risk genes (Benthall et al., 2021; Fuccillo, 2016; Peça et al., 2011; Peixoto et al., 2016; Platt et al., 2017; Rothwell et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Prior studies have demonstrated changes in striatal function and striatum-associated behaviors in mice with mutations in ASD risk genes.
source: The basal ganglia, in particular the striatum, represents one such commonly altered brain region, and prior studies have demonstrated changes in striatal function and striatum-associated behaviors in mice with mutations in ASD risk genes (Benthall et al., 2021; Fuccillo, 2016; Peça et al., 2011; Peixoto et al., 2016; Platt et al., 2017; Rothwell et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cntnap2 codes for a neurexin-like cell adhesion molecule called Contactin-associated protein-like 2 (Caspr2).
source: Cntnap2 codes for a neurexin-like cell adhesion molecule called Contactin-associated protein-like 2 (Caspr2; Poliak et al., 1999; Poliak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Poliak et al., 1999 and 2003.

claim: Caspr2 is expressed in several cortical and subcortical regions, including the striatum, from embryonic day 14 (E14) onward into adulthood in mice.
source: In mice, Caspr2 is expressed in several cortical and subcortical regions, including the striatum, from embryonic day 14 (E14) onward into adulthood (Peñagarikano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claim: Caspr2 is primarily localized at the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons.
source: Caspr2 is primarily localized at the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons and is involved in the clustering of potassium channels (Poliak et al., 2003; Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Poliak et al., 2003 and Scott et al., 2019.

claim: Caspr2 is involved in the clustering of potassium channels.
source: Caspr2 is primarily localized at the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons and is involved in the clustering of potassium channels (Poliak et al., 2003; Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Poliak et al., 2003 and Scott et al., 2019.

claim: In vitro studies in mice suggest that Caspr2 may play a role in AMPAR trafficking and cell morphology.
source: In vitro studies in mice suggest that Caspr2 may also play a role in AMPAR trafficking and cell morphology (Anderson et al., 2012; Gdalyahu et al., 2015; Varea et al., 2015), and ex vivo experiments indicate that it can control cell excitability and circuit synchronicity (Martín-de-Saavedra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2012; Gdalyahu et al., 2015; Varea et al., 2015.

claim: Ex vivo experiments indicate that Caspr2 can control cell excitability and circuit synchronicity.
source: In vitro studies in mice suggest that Caspr2 may also play a role in AMPAR trafficking and cell morphology (Anderson et al., 2012; Gdalyahu et al., 2015; Varea et al., 2015), and ex vivo experiments indicate that it can control cell excitability and circuit synchronicity (Martín-de-Saavedra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martín-de-Saavedra et al., 2022.

claim: Caspr2 is important during neurodevelopment.
source: Caspr2 is important during neurodevelopment and has been implicated in neuronal migration (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), the maturation and function of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons (Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2018), and the timing of myelination (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Caspr2 has been implicated in neuronal migration.
source: Caspr2 is important during neurodevelopment and has been implicated in neuronal migration (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), the maturation and function of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons (Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2018), and the timing of myelination (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claim: Caspr2 has been implicated in the maturation and function of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons.
source: Caspr2 is important during neurodevelopment and has been implicated in neuronal migration (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), the maturation and function of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons (Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2018), and the timing of myelination (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2018.

claim: Caspr2 has been implicated in the timing of myelination.
source: Caspr2 is important during neurodevelopment and has been implicated in neuronal migration (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), the maturation and function of parvalbumin-positive GABAergic interneurons (Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2018), and the timing of myelination (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 2019.

claim: CNTNAP2 mutations in people lead to a neurodevelopmental syndrome that can include language disorders, epilepsy, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and ASD.
source: CNTNAP2 mutations in people lead to a neurodevelopmental syndrome that can include language disorders, epilepsy, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and ASD (Peñagarikano and Geschwind, 2012; Rodenas-Cuadrado et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peñagarikano and Geschwind, 2012; Rodenas-Cuadrado et al., 2014.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit good face validity for ASD-relevant social and motor behavior alterations.
source: A mouse model of this syndrome, Cntnap2-/-, has been shown to exhibit good face validity for ASD-relevant social and motor behavior alterations (Brunner et al., 2015; Dawes et al., 2018; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brunner et al., 2015; Dawes et al., 2018; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2019.

claim: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs).
source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SPNs make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the direct pathway (dSPNs) and the indirect pathway (iSPNs).
source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: dSPNs express D1-receptors and project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: iSPNs express D2-receptors and project to external globus pallidus (GPe).
source: The striatum is primarily composed of GABAergic striatal projection neurons (SPNs), which make up two functionally distinct output pathways: the D1-receptor expressing cells of the direct pathway (dSPNs), which project to substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), and the D2-receptor expressing cells of the indirect pathway (iSPNs), which project to external globus pallidus (GPe; Calabresi et al., 2014; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SPNs receive excitatory glutamatergic inputs from cortex and thalamus, as well as dopaminergic input from the midbrain.
source: The two types of SPNs are intermixed throughout the striatum and receive excitatory glutamatergic inputs from cortex and thalamus, as well as dopaminergic input from the midbrain (Ding et al., 2008; Doig et al., 2010; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Coordinated activity between the populations of SPNs mediates action selection, motor learning, and habit formation.
source: Coordinated activity between the populations of SPNs in response to these inputs mediates action selection, motor learning, and habit formation (Hawes et al., 2015; Santos et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: SPNs comprise upwards of 95% of the cells in the striatum.
source: Although SPNs comprise upwards of 95% of the cells in the striatum, there are distinct types of GABAergic interneurons that contribute significantly to the inhibitory circuitry of the striatum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about striatal composition.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons, which make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum, provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs (Burke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burke et al., 2017.

claim: PV interneurons provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons, which make up ~2% of the cells in the striatum, provide the largest feedforward inhibition onto SPNs (Burke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burke et al., 2017.

claim: Changes in the number and/or function of PV interneurons have been identified in several ASD mouse models, including Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Changes in the number and/or function of PV interneurons have been identified in several ASD mouse models, including Cntnap2-/- mice, implicating PV circuitry as a potential common alteration across ASD mouse models (Filice et al., 2020; Juarez and Martínez Cerdeño, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filice et al., 2020; Juarez and Martínez Cerdeño, 2022.

claim: dSPNs in Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited increased spike probability compared to wild-type (WT) dSPNs.
source: We quantified the number of evoked APs at different light intensities and found that dSPNs in young adult Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited increased spike probability compared to wild-type (WT) dSPNs (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The interaction effect of genotype and stimulation intensity in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs suggests increased corticostriatal drive.
source: The interaction effect of genotype and stimulation intensity in these cells suggests increased corticostriatal drive, consistent with findings in another mouse model with loss of function of the ASD-risk gene Tsc1 (Benthall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by comparison to another study.

claim: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs had subtly increased cortically-evoked AP firing compared to WT iSPNs, although this was not statistically significant.
source: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs had subtly increased cortically-evoked AP firing compared to WT iSPNs, although this was not statistically significant (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The average optically evoked EPSC amplitude was not significantly different across a range of light intensities in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT.
source: We found that the average optically evoked EPSC amplitude was not significantly different across a range of light intensities in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: There were no significant differences in AMPA:NMDA ratio in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs.
source: In an additional group of mice, we measured the ratio of AMPAR currents recorded at −70 mV to NMDAR currents recorded at +40 mV (at 20% blue light intensity) and found no significant differences in AMPA:NMDA ratio in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs (Figure 1J–M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-M.

claim: Cntnap2-/- SPNs in adult mice had similar spine density as WT.
source: We found that Cntnap2-/- SPNs in adult mice had similar spine density as WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting no overall change in synapse number.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enhanced cortically driven spiking in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs is not due to a change in corticostriatal synaptic strength or overall synapse density.
source: Together, these results show that dSPNs in Cntnap2-/- mice exhibit enhanced cortically driven spiking. However, this is not due to a change in corticostriatal synaptic strength or overall synapse density.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Previous work has indicated a reduction in the number and/or function of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across multiple brain regions in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Previous work has indicated a reduction in the number and/or function of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across multiple brain regions in Cntnap2-/- mice (Ahmed et al., 2023; Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015; Paterno et al., 2021; Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus of Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: While deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus (Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015), and the number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), a comprehensive assessment of striatal inhibitory synaptic function has yet to be completed in Cntnap2-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015.

claim: The number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: While deficits in inhibition have been identified in the cortex and hippocampus (Antoine et al., 2019; Jurgensen and Castillo, 2015), and the number of PV interneurons has been reported to be decreased in the striatum (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), a comprehensive assessment of striatal inhibitory synaptic function has yet to be completed in Cntnap2-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claim: In Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs, the average amplitude of electrically evoked IPSCs across a range of stimulation intensities was not different from WT.
source: In Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs, the average amplitude of electrically evoked IPSCs across a range of stimulation intensities was not different from WT (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: The average amplitude of optically-evoked IPSCs did not differ significantly in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT controls.
source: We found that the average amplitude of optically-evoked IPSCs did not differ significantly in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs or iSPNs compared to WT controls (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: There were no significant differences in the intrinsic excitability of PV interneurons in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to controls.
source: Plotting the number of APs fired as a function of current step amplitude indicated that there were no significant differences in the intrinsic excitability of PV interneurons in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There were no changes in intrinsic cell properties such as rheobase, membrane resistance, capacitance, resting membrane potential, or AP shape in Cntnap2-/- PV interneurons.
source: There were also no changes in intrinsic cell properties such as rheobase, membrane resistance, capacitance, resting membrane potential, or AP shape in Cntnap2-/- PV interneurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-K.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of PV-positive cells in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT.
source: We found no significant difference in the number of PV-positive cells in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F and K–N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F and K-N.

claim: There were no changes in the average single cell or total level of PV protein expression in the dorsal striatum of Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: We also found no changes in the average single cell or total level of PV protein expression in the dorsal striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-J.

claim: There were no significant changes in PV interneuron number, PV expression, or PV interneuron-mediated inhibition in the adult Cntnap2-/- striatum compared to WT controls.
source: Overall, we did not observe significant changes in PV interneuron number, PV expression, or PV interneuron-mediated inhibition in the adult Cntnap2-/- striatum compared to WT controls.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had significantly increased intrinsic excitability compared to WT dSPNs.
source: We found that Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had significantly increased intrinsic excitability compared to WT dSPNs (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had reduced rheobase current.
source: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs also had reduced rheobase current (Figure 3C), the minimum current required to evoke an AP, as well as increased membrane resistance (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs had increased membrane resistance.
source: Cntnap2-/- dSPNs also had reduced rheobase current (Figure 3C), the minimum current required to evoke an AP, as well as increased membrane resistance (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a trend towards increased excitability in Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, but this effect was not statistically significant.
source: While there was a trend towards increased excitability in Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3G–H), and these cells did not exhibit changes in rheobase current (Figure 3I) or membrane resistance (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Cntnap2-/- iSPNs did not exhibit changes in rheobase current or membrane resistance.
source: While there was a trend towards increased excitability in Cntnap2-/- iSPNs, this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3G–H), and these cells did not exhibit changes in rheobase current (Figure 3I) or membrane resistance (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Membrane capacitance, resting membrane potential, and AP shape were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs.
source: Membrane capacitance (Figure 3E and K), resting membrane potential (Figure 3F and L), and AP shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs, although latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, K, F, L, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: Membrane capacitance (Figure 3E and K), resting membrane potential (Figure 3F and L), and AP shape (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were not significantly changed in Cntnap2-/- SPNs, although latency to first spike was reduced in both Cntnap2-/- dSPNs and iSPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and I.

claim: The increase in dSPN intrinsic excitability likely underlies the enhanced corticostriatal drive in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Given the lack of synaptic changes observed in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs, the increase in dSPN intrinsic excitability likely underlies their enhanced corticostriatal drive (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Caspr2 is known to be involved in the clustering of voltage-gated potassium channels, particularly Kv1.2 channels.
source: Caspr2 is known to be involved in the clustering of voltage-gated potassium channels (Inda et al., 2006; Poliak et al., 1999; Poliak et al., 2003), particularly Kv1.2 channels (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Kv1.2 channels play an important role in regulating the intrinsic excitability of SPNs.
source: These channels play an important role in regulating the intrinsic excitability of SPNs (Nisenbaum et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nisenbaum et al., 1994.

claim: Blockade of Kv1.2 channels with α-Dendrotoxin (α-DTX) results in increased AP frequency, decreased rheobase current, decreased first AP latency, and decreased AP threshold, particularly in dSPNs.
source: Blockade of these channels with the drug α-Dendrotoxin (α-DTX) results in increased AP frequency, decreased rheobase current, decreased first AP latency, and decreased AP threshold (Shen et al., 2004), particularly in dSPNs (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shen et al., 2004 and Lahiri and Bevan, 2020.

claim: α-DTX enhanced AP firing and decreased AP threshold in WT dSPNs, but not in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
source: We found that α-DTX enhanced AP firing and decreased AP threshold in WT dSPNs (Figure 4A–C), but not in Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: AP width was significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
source: AP width was also significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q), while AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q.

claim: AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased by α-DTX in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
source: AP width was also significantly increased by α-DTX in WT but not Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Q), while AP fast afterhyperpolarization and AP latency were significantly decreased in both WT and Cntnap2-/- dSPNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, I, N and R.

claim: The effects of α-DTX on Cntnap2-/- dSPNs are largely occluded, indicating that Kv1.2 channels are basally altered by loss of Cntnap2.
source: Together, these data show that the effects of α-DTX on Cntnap2-/- dSPNs are largely occluded, indicating that Kv1.2 channels are basally altered by loss of Cntnap2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Altered Kv1.2 channels likely account for the enhanced intrinsic excitability of Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
source: This likely accounts for the enhanced intrinsic excitability of Cntnap2-/- dSPNs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: α-DTX had minimal effects on WT and Cntnap2-/- iSPNs.
source: We tested the effects of α-DTX on WT and Cntnap2-/- iSPNs and found minimal changes (Figure 4G–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), with no alterations in AP threshold (Figure 4I and L) and only a small shift in the input-output relationship of Cntnap2-/- iSPNs (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a difference in the sensitivity of dSPNs and iSPNs to Kv1 blockade.
source: The effects of α-DTX on iSPN excitability have been less well documented, and our data suggest a difference in the sensitivity of dSPNs and iSPNs to Kv1 blockade.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Alterations in striatal circuits are thought to be involved in the manifestation of RRBs.
source: RRBs comprise one of the primary symptom domains of ASD (APA, 2022). Alterations in striatal circuits are thought to be involved in the manifestation of RRBs, given the striatum's role in action selection and motor control (Estes et al., 2011; Fuccillo, 2016; Hollander et al., 2005; Langen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There was no significant difference in the total distance traveled, average speed, or number of rears in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT controls in the open field.
source: In the open field, we found no significant difference in the total distance traveled, average speed, or number of rears in Cntnap2-/- mice compared to WT controls (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more entries into the center of the open field arena than WT mice.
source: We did find that Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more entries into the center of the open field arena than WT mice, which may reflect a reduction in avoidance behavior in these mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice initiated more self-grooming bouts than WT controls in the open field.
source: Manually scored grooming behavior revealed that Cntnap2-/- mice initiated more self-grooming bouts than WT controls in the open field (Figure 5I), consistent with prior reports (Peñagarikano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and a citation to Peñagarikano et al., 2011.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice buried significantly more marbles on average than WT controls.
source: We found that Cntnap2-/- mice buried significantly more marbles on average than WT controls (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more nose pokes within a 10-min period than WT mice in the holeboard assay.
source: Cntnap2-/- mice made significantly more nose pokes within a 10-min period than WT mice (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Increased nose poking in Cntnap2-/- mice was largely due to increased poking during the last 5 min of the holeboard test.
source: This was largely due to increased poking during the last 5 min of the test (Figure 5L and M), indicating persistent poking behavior in Cntnap2-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L and M.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice did not exhibit changes in general locomotor activity compared to WT littermates.
source: Again, we found that Cntnap2-/- mice did not exhibit changes in general locomotor activity compared to WT littermates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two syllables associated with grooming were performed with significantly increased frequency in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Analysis of movement 'syllables' using Keypoint-MoSeq revealed that across the 25 most frequent syllables, two syllables associated with grooming were performed with significantly increased frequency in Cntnap2-/- mice (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice had an increase in the total number of grooming bouts.
source: Cntnap2-/- mice also had an increase in the total number of grooming bouts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), replicating the findings in the manually scored cohort (see Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited less entropy in syllable transitions, suggesting less variability in the transition from one movement syllable to the next.
source: A measure of the entropy of syllable transitions revealed that Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited less entropy, suggesting less variability in the transition from one movement syllable to the next (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Decoding models performed significantly better than chance at identifying WT and Cntnap2-/- mice based on their syllable usage and transitions, but not general locomotor activity.
source: The decoding models performed significantly better than chance at identifying WT and Cntnap2-/- mice based on their syllable usage and transitions, but not general locomotor activity (Figure 5P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5P.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice performed significantly better than WT mice in the accelerating rotarod task, particularly in the later trials when the rod rotates at the faster 10–80 RPM speed.
source: We found that Cntnap2-/- mice performed significantly better than WT mice in this task, particularly in the later trials when the rod rotates at the faster 10–80 RPM speed (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Initial performance (terminal velocity on trial one) was not significantly different between WT and Cntnap2-/- mice in the rotarod task.
source: Initial performance (terminal velocity on trial one) was not significantly different between WT and Cntnap2-/- mice (Figure 6C), but the learning rate from trial one to trial 12 was increased in Cntnap2-/- mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The learning rate from trial one to trial 12 was increased in Cntnap2-/- mice in the rotarod task.
source: Initial performance (terminal velocity on trial one) was not significantly different between WT and Cntnap2-/- mice (Figure 6C), but the learning rate from trial one to trial 12 was increased in Cntnap2-/- mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice showed no differences during the acquisition phase of the four-choice reversal learning task.
source: During acquisition, Cntnap2-/- mice performed similarly to WT controls, not differing in the average number of trials needed to reach criterion, the number of quadrant entries made before making a choice, or the latency to choose a pot (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited typical recall on day 2 of the four-choice reversal learning task.
source: On day 2, Cntnap2-/- mice exhibited typical recall, demonstrating successful consolidation of the odor-reward pairing (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice had a deficit in reversal learning, requiring significantly more trials on average than WTs to reach criterion once the odor-reward pairing was changed.
source: However, we found that Cntnap2-/- mice had a deficit in reversal learning, requiring significantly more trials on average than WTs to reach criterion once the odor-reward pairing was changed (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: During reversal, Cntnap2-/- mice made fewer quadrant entries before making a digging choice and had significantly decreased latency to make a choice compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, during reversal, Cntnap2-/- mice made fewer quadrant entries before making a digging choice and had significantly decreased latency to make a choice compared to controls (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: Even after the first correct choice of O2 during reversal, Cntnap2-/- mice took more trials to reach criterion than WTs.
source: Even after the first correct choice of O2 during reversal, Cntnap2-/- mice took more trials to reach criterion than WTs (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice made more reversal errors than WT mice, in particular perseverative and regressive errors.
source: In terms of errors, Cntnap2-/- mice made more reversal errors than WT mice (Figure 7J), in particular perseverative (continuing to choose O1) and regressive (choosing O1 after correctly choosing O2 once) errors (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J and K.

claim: Cntnap2-/- mice did not differ from WT controls in choices of the novel or irrelevant odors, or in the number of omitted trials.
source: Cntnap2-/- mice did not differ from WT controls in choices of the novel (newly introduced during reversal) or irrelevant (never rewarded) odors, or in the number of omitted trials (timing out without making a choice; Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The persistence in choosing O1, even after at least one correct choice of O2, drove the cognitive inflexibility in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Instead, the persistence in choosing O1, even after at least one correct choice of O2, drove the cognitive inflexibility in these mice (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: Loss of Cntnap2 resulted in a significant increase in the excitability of dSPNs, likely driven by altered contribution of Kv1.2 channels to intrinsic firing properties.
source: Instead, loss of Cntnap2 resulted in a significant increase in the excitability of dSPNs, likely driven by altered contribution of Kv1.2 channels to intrinsic firing properties.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings and inference.

claim: The loss of Caspr2 has a variable impact on intrinsic excitability across brain regions and cell types.
source: The loss of Caspr2 has a variable impact on intrinsic excitability across brain regions and cell types.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the discussion of various studies.

claim: The increased intrinsic excitability identified in dSPNs has also been observed in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and pyramidal cells of the cortex.
source: The increased intrinsic excitability that we identified in dSPNs has also been observed in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum (Fernández et al., 2021) and pyramidal cells of the cortex (Antoine et al., 2019; Cifuentes-Diaz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernández et al., 2021; Antoine et al., 2019; Cifuentes-Diaz et al., 2023.

claim: Hypoactivity or unchanged excitability of pyramidal cells has been observed in some cortical regions in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: However, we note hypoactivity (Brumback et al., 2018) or unchanged excitability (Lazaro et al., 2019) of pyramidal cells in some cortical regions in Cntnap2-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brumback et al., 2018 and Lazaro et al., 2019.

claim: There are profound deficits in the clustering of Kv1-family channels in Cntnap2-/- mice, particularly Kv1.2 channels.
source: Indeed, there are profound deficits in the clustering of Kv1-family channels in Cntnap2-/- mice, particularly Kv1.2 channels (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 2019.

claim: The loss of Caspr2 in Cntnap2-/- mice may result in improper localization of Kv1.2 channels, and thus alter their contribution to intrinsic excitability.
source: The loss of Caspr2 in Cntnap2-/- mice may result in improper localization of Kv1.2 channels, and thus alter their contribution to intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Blocking Kv1.2 channels has less of an effect on the excitability of iSPNs, which may account for the greater impact of Cntnap2 loss on dSPN physiology.
source: Interestingly, we find that blocking Kv1.2 channels has less of an effect on the excitability of iSPNs, which may account for the greater impact of Cntnap2 loss on dSPN physiology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Prior studies of Cntnap2-/- mice have identified changes in the number of PV-expressing interneurons in the cortex, hippocampus, and striatum.
source: Prior studies of Cntnap2-/- mice have identified changes in the number of PV-expressing interneurons in the cortex (Peñagarikano et al., 2011; Vogt et al., 2018), hippocampus (Paterno et al., 2021; Peñagarikano et al., 2011), and striatum (Peñagarikano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The finding of altered PV interneuron number is inconsistent across studies, as others have reported no change in the number of PV interneurons in these regions.
source: However, this finding is inconsistent across studies, as others have reported no change in the number of PV interneurons in these regions (Ahmed et al., 2023; Lauber et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2023; Lauber et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2019.

claim: One possible explanation for the disparity in PV interneuron counts is altered PV protein expression in Cntnap2-/- mice such that immunoreactivity varies in cell counting assessments.
source: One possible explanation for this disparity is altered PV protein expression in Cntnap2-/- mice such that immunoreactivity varies in cell counting assessments.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the inconsistent findings.

claim: The number of Vicia Villosa Agglutinin-positive (VVA+) perineuronal nets that preferentially surround PV cells is unchanged in Cntnap2-/- mice, even when PV immunoreactivity varies.
source: This is supported by the finding that the number of Vicia Villosa Agglutinin-positive (VVA+) perineuronal nets that preferentially surround PV cells is unchanged in Cntnap2-/- mice, even when PV immunoreactivity varies (Härtig et al., 1992; Haunsø et al., 2000; Lauber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Härtig et al., 1992; Haunsø et al., 2000; Lauber et al., 2018.

claim: Parvalbumin plays an important role in the intrinsic fast-spiking properties of PV interneurons, such that a reduction in PV protein expression is known to change PV intrinsic function.
source: Parvalbumin, a Ca2+ buffer, plays an important role in the intrinsic fast-spiking properties of PV interneurons, such that a reduction in PV protein expression is known to change PV intrinsic function (Orduz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orduz et al., 2013.

claim: Altered intrinsic properties of PV interneurons have been variably reported across brain regions and studies of Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: However, altered intrinsic properties of PV interneurons have also been variably reported across brain regions and studies of Cntnap2-/- mice, with subtle changes in PV firing properties reported in the developing striatum (Ahmed et al., 2023) and adult cortex (Vogt et al., 2018), but unchanged in the hippocampus (Paterno et al., 2021) and medial prefrontal cortex (Lazaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Primary changes in PV interneurons are unlikely to account for altered striatal circuit function in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: Together, this suggests that primary changes in PV interneurons are unlikely to account for altered striatal circuit function in Cntnap2-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The dorsal striatum can be subdivided into the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) and the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), with the former involved in goal-directed action-outcome learning and the latter implicated in the acquisition of habitual or procedural behaviors.
source: The dorsal striatum can be further subdivided into the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) and the DLS, with the former considered an associative region involved in goal-directed action-outcome learning and the latter implicated in the acquisition of habitual or procedural behaviors (Packard and Knowlton, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Packard and Knowlton, 2002.

claim: Learning and performance in the accelerating rotarod task have been associated with changes in the DLS.
source: In the accelerating rotarod assay, learning and performance in the task have been associated with changes in the DLS.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the rotarod task.

claim: Positive modulation of the firing rate of DLS neurons occurs during rotarod training, in particular in later trials of the task.
source: Positive modulation of the firing rate of DLS neurons occurs during rotarod training, in particular in later trials of the task, and synaptic potentiation of DLS SPNs in late training is necessary for intact performance (Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2009.

claim: Synaptic potentiation of DLS SPNs in late training is necessary for intact rotarod performance.
source: Positive modulation of the firing rate of DLS neurons occurs during rotarod training, in particular in later trials of the task, and synaptic potentiation of DLS SPNs in late training is necessary for intact performance (Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2009.

claim: Lesions of the DLS impair both early and late rotarod learning.
source: In line with this, lesions of the DLS impair both early and late rotarod learning (Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yin et al., 2009.

claim: Increased cortical drive of DLS dSPNs was sufficient to increase rotarod performance in another mouse model with disruption of an ASD-risk gene.
source: Functionally, we also found increased cortical drive of DLS dSPNs in these mice, a change that was sufficient to increase rotarod performance in another mouse model with disruption of an ASD-risk gene (Benthall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benthall et al., 2021.

claim: There is a connection between the change observed in DLS SPN physiology and the increased motor routine learning in Cntnap2-/- mice, although this idea remains to be causally tested.
source: Together, this supports a connection between the change observed in DLS SPN physiology and the increased motor routine learning in Cntnap2-/- mice, although this idea remains to be causally tested.
evidence: This is an inference that acknowledges the need for further causal testing.

claim: Early evidence implicates the striatum in the control of the syntax or sequence of movements in a rodent grooming bout.
source: Early evidence implicates the striatum in the control of the syntax or sequence of movements in a rodent grooming bout, such that very small lesions of DLS are capable of disrupting grooming (Cromwell and Berridge, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cromwell and Berridge, 1996.

claim: Recent work has outlined roles for cellular modulation in DMS and ventral striatal Islands of Calleja in the control of grooming behavior.
source: However, recent work has also outlined roles for cellular modulation in DMS and ventral striatal Islands of Calleja in the control of grooming behavior (Ramírez-Armenta et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramírez-Armenta et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Evidence linking increases in marble burying and nose poking behaviors to changes in cortico-striatal and amygdala-striatal function supports the notion that these behaviors may fit into a broader basal ganglia-associated RRB-like domain.
source: The precise neurobiological substrates of these behaviors are yet unclear, but evidence linking increases in these behaviors to changes in cortico-striatal and amygdala-striatal function supports the notion that these behaviors may fit into a broader basal ganglia-associated RRB-like domain (Albelda and Joel, 2012; Lee et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albelda and Joel, 2012; Lee et al., 2024.

claim: The DMS and ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) have been shown to play an important role in reversal learning.
source: The DMS and ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) have been shown to play an important role in reversal learning (Izquierdo et al., 2017), and in the four-choice task specifically (Delevich et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Izquierdo et al., 2017 and Delevich et al., 2022.

claim: Decreased dopamine release in the DLS is associated with deficits in reversal learning in the four-choice task.
source: Additionally, decreased dopamine release in the DLS is associated with deficits in reversal learning in this task (Kosillo et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kosillo et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2022.

claim: The learning phenotypes seen in Cntnap2-/- mice in the accelerating rotarod and reversal learning assay share an underlying rigidity in behavioral choice.
source: Together, the learning phenotypes seen in Cntnap2-/- mice in the accelerating rotarod and reversal learning assay share an underlying rigidity in behavioral choice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral findings.

claim: Changes in striatal circuits likely underlie the repetitive, stereotyped behaviors in Cntnap2-/- mice.
source: In both cases, changes in striatal circuits likely underlie the repetitive, stereotyped behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Divergent cellular changes in the striatum driven by a functionally diverse set of ASD risk genes similarly enhance corticostriatal drive, in particular, of the direct pathway.
source: In summary, our results fit into a model whereby divergent cellular changes in the striatum driven by a functionally diverse set of ASD risk genes similarly enhance corticostriatal drive, in particular, of the direct pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the findings.

claim: A shared gain-of-function in striatal circuits may play a role in the formation of perseverative or repetitive behaviors in a sub-set of ASDs more broadly.
source: We speculate that a shared gain-of-function in striatal circuits may play a role in the formation of perseverative or repetitive behaviors in a sub-set of ASDs more broadly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about broader implications.
